content: Fique, also known as Cabuya, is a natural fiber derived from the leaves of the fique plant, scientifically classified under the genus Furcraea. This plant is a xerophytic monocot native to the Andean regions of Colombia. From its origin, it spread to Venezuela and the eastern coast of Brazil. The fique plant is commonly referred to by various names, including Fique, Cabuya, Pita, Penca, Maguey, Cabui, Chuchao, or Coquiza. It is often mistaken for the agave plant, but the two can be distinguished by their leaves: agave leaves are yellowish, stiff, and have a strong spike at the tips, whereas fique leaves are droopy, greenish, and lack spikes. History Before the arrival of Spanish colonizers, pre-Columbian inhabitants had been extracting and utilizing fique fibers for centuries. They used these fibers to create garments, ropes, hammocks, and other items. In the 17th century, Dutch colonists transported the plant from their Brazilian colonies in Pernambuco to the island of Mauritius. The indigenous people of Mauritius adopted the fiber and referred to it as caraguatá-acú, croatá-acú, or gravata-acú. Fique fiber was subsequently introduced to other regions, including St. Helena, India, Sri Lanka, Algeria, Madagascar, East Africa, Mexico, and Costa Rica. In the 18th century, in Dagua, Valle del Cauca, Colombia, a priest named Feliciano Villalobos established the first industry for manufacturing ropes and wrapping materials using fique. By 1880, the Colombian government reported an annual production of three million kilograms of fique fibers, with two million kilograms exported to Venezuela. Additionally, five million pairs of alpargatas (traditional shoes) and four million meters of rope were fabricated from fique. However, between 1970 and 1975, the fique industry faced a significant decline due to the rise of polypropylene, a cheaper and faster-to-produce synthetic material. Today, fique is recognized as Colombia's national fiber and is used in ethnic products, handicrafts, and, more recently, in heat protectors for Colombian coffee cups sold in Juan Valdez coffee shops worldwide. Uses 1. Packing: Fique is primarily used in Colombia for manufacturing sacks and packaging materials for agricultural products. Depending on the thread density, the products are classified as: Dense (6,000–10,000 threads per square meter): Suitable for flour and small grains like rice. Semi-dense (4,800–5,500 threads per square meter): Used for larger grains such as coffee and beans. Loose (300–360 threads per square meter): Ideal for fruits, vegetables, and panela (unrefined cane sugar). 2. Ropes: Fique fibers are used to produce highly durable ropes and strings of various calibers, ranging from thin threads to one-inch-diameter manilas. These ropes are widely employed in industries such as transportation, construction, and sailing. 3. Pack animal accessories: Many items used for pack animals, such as enjalmas (saddle pads), cinchas (girths), retrancas (back straps), lazos (ropes), pretales (breast straps), tapa de enjalma (saddle covers), and cinchos (belts), are handmade using fique. 4. Tapestry: Mixed and raw fique fibers are used to create rugs and tapestries of varying sizes and qualities. These fibers can be combined with other organic materials, such as avocado seeds, achiote, and eucalyptus bark. 5. Other products: Fique is also used to make handicrafts, purses, bags, handbags, mattresses, curtains, shoes, umbrellas, baskets, and other items. Subproducts 1. Pulp: Used to produce organic fertilizers and paper. 2. Leaf juice: Utilized in the production of soap, fungicides, alcoholic beverages (homemade tapetusa), organic fuel, and animal feed. 3. Floral stem: The strong floral stem of the fique plant is used in constructing houses and ladders. 4. Bulbs: The terminal bulbs of the plant, when pickled, are edible. 5. Medicinal uses: Peasants use the leaves in topical preparations to treat boils. Leaf extracts are also used to combat horse lice. Cultivation Fique can be obtained from several species of Furcraea, including Furcraea macrophylla Baker, Furcraea cabuya Trel., Furcraea andina Trel., and Furcraea castilla. Depending on the processing method and the species used, various types of fique fibers can be produced. Main varieties: Ceniza (ash-colored) Espinosa (rough texture) Castilla or Golden Border Sisal Secondary varieties: Cabuya verde (green) Uña de águila (eagle nail) Negra común (black common) Chachagueña Genoia Tunosa común (common spiked) Jardineña Espadilla Rabo de chucha (opossum tail) Optimal growing conditions for the fique plant include: Temperature: 19–23°C Altitude: 1,300–1,900 meters Annual rainfall: 1,000–1,600 mm Sunlight: 5–6 hours per day Soil: Dry and rich in silicates Fique crops contribute nitrogen to the soil, enhancing its fertility. The plant is highly adaptable to various ecological conditions and can produce 1 to 6 kilograms of fibers annually. Diseases 1. Llaga Macana or Rayadilla: A viral disease that affects all varieties and parts of the fique plant, particularly in crops grown above 1,900 meters in altitude. There is no chemical control for this disease, and it must be managed through preventive measures. 2. Pink Disease: Caused by the fungus Corticium salmonicolor, this disease damages the leaves and disrupts the fibers. Treatment involves the use of copper-based fungicides. Peasants also treat this disease by applying ashes to the base of the leaves. 3. Leaf Cochineal (Diaspis bromelia): Caused by a parasitic insect. 4. Leaf Beetle: A beetle that perforates the base of the leaves.
